## Abstract {.unnumbered}

The PISCO gridded climate product for Peru provides daily dew-point temperature (Td) only through
2016, while its minimum-temperature (Tmin) record continues to 2020. This leaves a four-year gap in
a variable required for agricultural and hydrological modelling. We extend the Td record to
2017–2020 by learning a Tmin→Td mapping on the 1981–2016 overlap and applying it forward at every
grid cell. The model is a per-(cell, day-of-year) weighted local linear regression on climate
anomalies, in which both the predictor set and the day-of-year smoothing half-window are selected
per **SENAMHI climate zone × day-of-year** by leave-one-year-out cross-validation, following the
MultiLLR approach of @hwang2019. Because no observed Td exists in the gap, prediction is
**autoregressive**: each predicted day feeds the following day's Td lags.

Validation is **temporal, not spatial**: we hold out the most recent four years (train 1981–2012,
predict 2013–2016) and score against observed Td under the same autoregressive conditions the real
gap imposes. The tuned model attains RMSE 1.219 °C versus 1.535 °C for climatology — the incumbent
gap-filling choice — a reduction of 0.316 °C [95% CI 0.314, 0.317], skill 0.206, outperforming
climatology at 99.99% of grid cells (Cohen's *d* = 2.98, permutation *p* ≈ 2×10⁻⁴). It also beats
Td = Tmin (FAO-56) by 2.33 °C and a per-zone OLS fit by 1.11 °C. Re-selecting recipes on training
years only changes skill by 0.009, confirming the result is not an artefact of selection.

The resulting product covers 2,178,827 grid cells × 1,461 days (3.18 × 10⁹ values). It shows no
discontinuity at the 2016/2017 boundary: over equal-length four-year windows the filled field
differs from the last observed window (mean −0.041 °C, sd 0.176 °C) no more than two observed
windows differ from each other (mean +0.101 °C, sd 0.125 °C), with no grid cell exceeding 1 °C in
either comparison. A known limitation is a small warm tail (0.13% of values > 35 °C) confined to
the north-eastern Amazon lowlands and concentrated almost entirely in **November**, the dry-to-wet
transition (1.56% of November values versus 0.03% in October). Diagnostics over all 3.18 × 10⁹ values rule out autoregressive error accumulation as
the cause and point instead to a regime-dependent breakdown of the Tmin–Td coupling. **[SME]**

## Introduction

Dew-point temperature is a primary input to reference-evapotranspiration, disease-risk and
crop-growth models. For Peru, the PISCO family of gridded products [@huerta2022] provides the
national-scale daily fields these applications need. However, the products are versioned and
released asynchronously: dew point is available from the v1.1 release for **1981–2016**, whereas
minimum temperature has been extended in v1.2 to **1981–2020**. Applications requiring Td after
2016 therefore face a four-year gap.

The standard fallbacks are unattractive. Substituting the **daily climatology** discards all
interannual and synoptic information. The FAO-56 approximation **Td ≈ Tmin** [@allen1998] is
convenient but biased in arid and high-altitude terrain. A single national regression of Td on Tmin
ignores the extreme heterogeneity of Peruvian microclimates, which span hyper-arid coast, high
Andes and humid Amazon within a few hundred kilometres.

We therefore ask a narrow, answerable question: **can the Tmin→Td relationship learned on the
1981–2016 overlap reconstruct Td for 2017–2020 more accurately than these incumbents?** Two
features distinguish this from a conventional spatial-interpolation problem:

1. **It predicts new *years* at the *same* grid cells**, not new locations. Validation must
   therefore be temporal (hold out years), not spatial (hold out sites).
2. **No observed Td exists in the gap.** Because the model uses Td lags as predictors, prediction
   must be autoregressive, and any honest validation must be run the same way.

A negative result would have been publishable: if per-zone tuning failed to beat a strong
climatology under these conditions, that would itself be a useful finding, provided the baselines
and validation were rigorous. It does not fail.

## Data {#sec-data}

| Item | Source | Coverage | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Dew point Td | PISCO **v1.1** | 1981–2016 | Target (the record being extended) |
| Minimum temperature Tmin | PISCO **v1.2** | 1981–2020 | Predictor (train **and** predict) |
| Grid | PISCO national grid | 2,818,404 cells | Model domain |
| Climate zones | SENAMHI Thornthwaite classification | 41 zones | Unit of model selection |

: Data inventory. {#tbl-data}

**Version consistency (important).** Tmin v1.1 and v1.2 differ enough that mixing them injects a
systematic bias: the fitted Tmin sensitivity differs by version (coefficient mean 0.45 vs 0.37) and
switching versions between training and prediction shifts Td by ≈0.3 °C. We therefore use **v1.2
Tmin on both sides** — training and prediction — so the mapping is applied to the same data
generating process it was learned from.

**Grid alignment (important).** The raw v1.2 Tmin distribution is supplied on a 302,449-point
subset grid whose cell indices do **not** correspond to those of the 2,818,404-cell national grid
used by the Td product. Applying it directly produces physically meaningless results (we measured a
spurious −8.7 °C step at the 2016/2017 boundary). All future Tmin was therefore re-extracted onto
the full national grid; we verified the resulting grid index is byte-identical to that of the Td
product.

Of the 2,818,404 cells, **2,178,827** (77.3%) yield predictions; the remainder are ocean or
otherwise lack the climatology or Tmin required by the model.

**Caveat on the target.** Validation is against the *gridded* v1.1 Td, which is the product being
extended — the appropriate reference for this task. Gridded Td and Tmin both derive from land
surface temperature and elevation covariates in the PISCOeo_pm framework [@huerta2022], so they
share some structure; Td is not derived from Tmin directly. Station-level validation is out of
scope (@sec-limitations).

## Methods {#sec-methods}

### Anomaly formulation

All modelling is performed on **anomalies** relative to a per-(cell, day-of-year) daily
climatology computed over the training years:

$$ X_{\text{anom}}(t) = X(t) - \bar{X}(\mathrm{doy}(t)) $$

For each cell and day-of-year the model is a weighted local linear regression

$$ \mathrm{Td}_{\text{anom}}(t) = \beta_0 + \sum_k \beta_k \, x_k(t) + \varepsilon $$

where candidate predictors $x_k$ are drawn from the pool
$\{\mathrm{TMIN\_anom}, \mathrm{TMIN\_anom\_lag}_{1,2,7,30}, \mathrm{TD\_anom\_lag}_{1,2,3,7,30}\}$
plus an intercept (11 candidates). Td enters only through lags, never contemporaneously. Fitting
uses a circular tricube kernel over day-of-year with half-window $h$, so each (cell, doy) model
borrows strength from nearby days of year across all training years.

### Per-zone × day-of-year model selection {#sec-selection}

Rather than fixing the predictor set and $h$ globally, we select both **per SENAMHI climate zone ×
day-of-year** (41 × 366 = 15,006 recipes), following the multitask MultiLLR design of @hwang2019:
predictors are chosen jointly across grid points within a zone, while coefficients are fitted per
grid point. Selection is by **backward-stepwise elimination** under a **leave-one-year-out
cross-validated (LOYOCV) cosine-skill** objective, with $h$ searched over $\{7, 11, 15, 21, 31,
45\}$ days.

Selection runs on a stratified sample of **66,534 cells** (target 2,000 per zone) — sufficient to
*choose* a recipe, since LOYOCV skill sums are additive across cell chunks — not on the full grid.

### Training

The selected recipes are then applied to fit coefficients at **all 2,818,404 grid cells** in a
single pass, each (cell, doy) using its zone's recipe as a feature mask. This yields
8.13 × 10⁹ tidy coefficient rows.

### Autoregressive forecast {#sec-forecast}

For 2017–2020 no observed Td exists, so `TD_anom_lag`$_k$ predictors must be supplied by the
model's own earlier predictions. The forecast is seeded with observed Td from December 2016 and
advances day by day: the value predicted on day $t$ becomes an input for days $t+1 \ldots t+k$.
Tmin predictors are exogenous and observed throughout, so they require no recursion. This
sequential dependence is intrinsic to the method, not an implementation limitation.

### Implementation

Selection and training are GPU-accelerated (CuPy, single NVIDIA RTX A2000 12 GB); the grid is
partitioned into 8,192 buckets so per-bucket tensors fit in device memory. Full-grid selection plus
training took ≈39.5 h wall-clock. The production fill parallelises across buckets on 14 CPU
processes and completes in ≈20 min. Code: `HPC_code_tunning/` (see @sec-availability).

## Validation design {#sec-validation}

The evaluation must answer: *how accurate will the 2017–2020 fill be?* Since that answer cannot be
observed, we reproduce its conditions on years we can score.

- **Forward temporal hold-out.** Train on early years, predict the most recent years, score against
  observed Td. The headline split is **leave-last-4** (train 1981–2012, predict 2013–2016),
  mirroring the real four-year gap; leave-last-1 and leave-last-2 give the lead-time curve.
- **Autoregressive throughout.** No observed Td enters the held-out block, exactly as in production.
- **No leakage.** Climatology — used both as a baseline and as the anomaly anchor — is recomputed on
  training years only.
- **Baseline ladder**, scored on the identical hold-out: climatology, Td = Tmin [@allen1998],
  per-zone OLS Td~Tmin, and the tuned model. We use the **uncorrected** FAO-56 form; established
  aridity-dependent corrections exist [@kimball1997; @eccel2012] and a −2 °C offset is common
  practice in arid and semi-arid settings [@huang2024]. Over our domain the uncorrected form is the
  *more favourable* variant — its measured bias is −2.13 °C (it under-predicts observed Td), so a
  further −2 °C offset would increase the error — but a regionally applied correction (coast and
  Andes only) would be the fairer comparison and is left for future work. **[TODO]**
- **Sample.** 64 whole buckets = 17,041 cells. Because bucket assignment is `ID mod 8192`, each
  bucket is a nationwide lattice spanning all 41 zones, making a few buckets a cheap, representative
  sample.
- **Effect sizes over p-values.** ΔRMSE in °C with location-block bootstrap 95% CIs, skill score,
  fraction of cells improved, Cohen's *d*, and a sign-flip permutation null (5,000 draws).

**Selection honesty.** In the primary run the *recipe* came from the full-period manifest, which had
seen the hold-out. We therefore repeated the exercise re-selecting recipes on training years only;
the difference bounds the selection optimism (@sec-results-validation).

## Results {#sec-results}

### Model selection {#sec-results-selection}

Selection retains most candidates — the full 11-predictor set is kept for 70.7% of zone-days, and no
predictor is retained in fewer than 91% of recipes — indicating that the conventional fixed
five-predictor configuration is *under*-specified. The chosen half-window distributes across the
whole grid ($h$ = 7: 14.2%, 11: 9.2%, 15: 9.4%, 21: 11.1%, 31: 13.0%, 45: 43.1%). That $h = 45$ is
modal is itself a finding: the model prefers broad day-of-year pooling, trading seasonal specificity
for sample size. Extending the grid beyond 21 days was worthwhile but second-order (hold-out skill
0.197 → 0.200).

In-sample LOYOCV uplift over the fixed five-predictor baseline is small (mean +0.015, median +0.008
skill; 16.8% of zone-days show no gain). **These in-sample numbers are selection-optimistic and are
not the headline** — @sec-results-validation is.

![Model-selection diagnostics: distribution of the selected day-of-year half-window $h$, predictor
retention, and LOYOCV skill uplift over the fixed-5 baseline.](figures/S1_manifest_overview.png){#fig-manifest}

### Temporal validation {#sec-results-validation}

The tuned model outperforms every incumbent at every lead time (@tbl-ladder, @fig-ladder).

| Split (train → predict) | Climatology | Td = Tmin | Zone OLS | **Tuned** | Skill vs clim. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ll1 (1981–2015 → 2016)     | 1.680 | 3.621 | 2.379 | **1.262** | **0.249** |
| ll2 (1981–2014 → 2015–16)  | 1.667 | 3.676 | 2.370 | **1.274** | **0.235** |
| **ll4 (1981–2012 → 2013–16)** | **1.535** | **3.551** | **2.329** | **1.219** | **0.206** |

: Hold-out RMSE (°C), pooled over all held-out cell-days (ll4: *n* = 24,896,901). {#tbl-ladder}

For the headline ll4 split, paired per-cell effect sizes (17,041 cells):

| Tuned vs | ΔRMSE °C [95% CI] | Skill | Cells improved | Cohen's *d* | perm. *p* |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Climatology | +0.316 [0.314, 0.317] | 0.206 | 99.99% | 2.98 | 2×10⁻⁴ |
| Td = Tmin   | +2.332 [2.308, 2.354] | 0.657 | 99.98% | 1.37 | 2×10⁻⁴ |
| Zone OLS    | +1.110 [1.091, 1.126] | 0.476 | 99.80% | 1.06 | 2×10⁻⁴ |

: Effect sizes, ll4 split. CIs from location-block bootstrap. {#tbl-effects}

The tuned model shows bias −0.046 °C and *r* = 0.990. Skill declines monotonically with lead time
(0.249 → 0.235 → 0.206), the expected growth of error under autoregression, without collapsing over
a four-year horizon (@fig-leadtime).

**Selection bias is negligible.** Re-selecting recipes on training years only lowers ll4 skill from
0.206 to 0.197 — a difference of 0.009 skill (≈0.013 °C RMSE, ~4% of the uplift). The advantage over
climatology is therefore a property of the method, not of having seen the hold-out.

**Seasonal bias is corrected.** The fixed-configuration model carries a +1.45 °C December warm bias;
under the per-zone × day-of-year recipes the December bias falls to +0.01 °C, with all months within
±0.44 °C.

![Hold-out RMSE ladder, ll4 split: the tuned model against the three
incumbents.](figures/S2_rmse_ladder_ll4.png){#fig-ladder}

![Skill versus climatology as a function of forecast lead
time.](figures/S2_lead_time_curve.png){#fig-leadtime}

### The gap-filled product {#sec-results-product}

Applying the coefficients trained on all of 1981–2016 to the observed 2017–2020 Tmin yields
**3,183,266,247** predicted values over 2,178,827 cells and 1,461 days, with no missing values.
National mean Td is 19.39 °C (range −13.29 to 41.16 °C); annual means are stable across the horizon
(19.36, 19.30, 19.41, 19.51 °C for 2017–2020), showing no drift under sustained autoregression.

The filled field reproduces the expected national structure — a humid Amazon (~25 °C), a sharply
delineated cold Andean cordillera, and the coastal gradient (@fig-map) — and continues the observed
seasonal cycle across the 2016/2017 boundary with matching amplitude and phase (@fig-timeseries).

![National monthly-mean Td, 2010–2020: observed (blue, through 2016) and gap-filled (red,
2017–2020).](figures/F1_national_td_timeseries_seam.png){#fig-timeseries}

![Mean gap-filled Td, 2017–2020.](figures/F2_meanTd_map_2017_2020.png){#fig-map}

### Seam continuity {#sec-results-seam}

A gap-filled record must not introduce an artificial step where prediction begins. Comparing
adjacent *months* across the boundary conflates the real seasonal cycle with any such step, so we
test on **equal-length full-year windows**, which removes seasonality, and include a **model-free
control**: the difference between two consecutive observed four-year windows, which measures the
natural period-to-period variability of the observed record itself.

| Comparison | Mean | sd | 1st–99th pct | Cells \|Δ\| > 1 °C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** obs 2013–16 − obs 2009–12 *(control, no model)* | +0.101 | 0.125 | −0.18 … +0.42 | 0.0% |
| **B** pred 2017–20 − obs 2013–16 *(seam)* | −0.041 | 0.176 | −0.36 … +0.54 | 0.0% |

: Difference in annual-mean Td (°C), 2,178,827 cells. {#tbl-seam}

The filled years differ from the last observed window no more than two observed windows differ from
each other: B's spread is 1.4× A's, its mean is closer to zero, and **no cell in either comparison
differs by more than 1 °C**. Panel B is spatially smooth and coherent, without the blockiness or
speckle that a numerical artefact would produce (@fig-seam).

![Seam artefact test on equal-length full-year windows. **A** natural variability (observed only);
**B** the seam; **C** distributions.](figures/F3_seam_artifact_test.png){#fig-seam}

## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

### Relation to existing humidity-from-temperature methods

The FAO-56 identity Td ≈ Tmin [@allen1998] is a starting point rather than the state of the art.
Its bias in arid, semi-arid and high-elevation terrain is well documented, and several corrections
are in routine use: an aridity-dependent adjustment driven by precipitation and potential
evapotranspiration [@kimball1997], a correction from temperature and precipitation validated across
alpine stations [@eccel2012], and a simple −2 °C offset widely applied in arid and semi-arid regions
[@huang2024]. Disaggregation frameworks such as MELODIST implement both the naive identity and
fitted regression alternatives precisely because the identity fails in a site- and regime-specific
way [@forster2016].

The most directly relevant prior result is @althoff2022, who calibrate the temperature-based
Penman-Monteith approach over the Brazilian Cerrado — a tropical biome with a pronounced dry season
— and find **corrections of opposite sign in the two seasons**: −0.93 °C in the wet season
(Td > Tmin) versus +0.57 °C in the dry season (Td < Tmin). The Tmin–Td coupling is therefore not a
fixed offset but a *regime-dependent* relationship. Our per-(zone × day-of-year) design can be read
as a generalisation of that finding: rather than two seasonal offsets for one biome, we fit a
separate local regression for each climate zone and each day of the year. The magnitude of our
improvement over both Td = Tmin (+2.33 °C RMSE) and a per-zone OLS fit (+1.11 °C) is consistent
with this interpretation — a single global or even per-zone linear relationship is too rigid.

### What the selected smoothing windows imply

Selection favours wide day-of-year windows, with *h* = 45 days modal at 43.1% (@fig-manifest). An
independent precedent exists: @chabotcouture2014 interpolate dew point with day-of-year-dependent
parameters smoothed over **31-day** windows, a comparable scale. The physical reading is that the
Tmin–Td relationship varies smoothly with day of year, so pooling neighbouring days buys sample size
at little cost in bias — the model prefers more data over finer seasonal resolution.

That preference is not free, however. Given @althoff2022's seasonal sign reversal, broad pooling
risks *blending distinct moisture regimes* into a single fitted slope. We return to this in
@sec-limitations, because it is the most plausible explanation for our one substantive failure mode.

### Positioning relative to the gap-filling literature

Most work described as "gap filling" reconstructs values **missing inside** an existing record —
station outages, sensor dropouts, cloud-obscured retrievals — using the surrounding observations in
space and time [e.g. @serranonotivoli2019]. Our problem is different in kind: **temporal
extrapolation beyond the end of the record**, where the target variable is unobserved *everywhere*
throughout the prediction window. No contemporaneous Td exists anywhere in 2017–2020 to interpolate
from.

This distinction has a direct methodological consequence. Spatial cross-validation — the prevailing
validation strategy, for instance the spatial leave-one-out used in global spatio-temporal
regression kriging of daily temperature [@kilibarda2014] — cannot measure the quantity we care
about, because it holds out *locations* while retaining contemporaneous observations. Only a forward
temporal hold-out reproduces the operational situation. Explicit comparisons of the two designs, and
systematic reporting of incumbent baselines such as climatology and persistence, remain uncommon in
this literature. We therefore treat the temporal hold-out as primary and report the full baseline
ladder with effect sizes and confidence intervals (@sec-results-validation).

### Autoregressive stability

Because Td lags are predictors and no observed Td exists in the gap, the forecast is a 1,461-step
recursion. The deep-learning climate literature documents that such rollouts can degrade
progressively or diverge outright through error accumulation, and that explicit multi-step training
is needed to stabilise them [@gallusser2025]. We see no comparable degradation: skill decays
gracefully with lead time (0.249 → 0.235 → 0.206 from one to four years, @fig-leadtime), annual mean
Td is stable to within 0.21 °C across the four filled years, and the incidence of extreme values is
**non-monotonic** in time rather than growing (@sec-limitations).

Two features of the design likely account for this. First, the dominant predictors are anomalies of
**observed, exogenous** Tmin, which are supplied from data at every step and never recurse; only the
Td-lag channel is autoregressive. Second, predictions are formed as anomalies added back to a fixed
per-cell climatology, which anchors the recursion to a physically sensible level. Free-running
emulators that must propagate their entire state forward have neither property. This suggests a
general point: **hybrid recursions with observed exogenous forcing and a climatological anchor are
substantially more stable over long horizons than fully autoregressive ones**, and the stability
concerns of that literature do not transfer directly to this class of model.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

**Warm tail. [SME]** 0.1326% of predicted values exceed 35 °C (maximum 41.16 °C), which is not
physically plausible for dew point. We characterised this failure mode over all 3.18 × 10⁹ values;
the diagnostics constrain its cause more tightly than the raw rate suggests.

*Where and when.* The affected cells (132,920 with at least one exceedance) lie in the
north-eastern Amazon lowlands, and the exceedances are concentrated almost entirely in a **single
month — November** — in every year: 2.41% of values in November 2017, 1.91% in November 2018, 1.55%
in November 2020 and 0.36% in November 2019, against 0.081% for the next-worst month (October 2018)
and below 0.03% elsewhere. Pooling the four years by month of year sharpens the picture further
(@fig-warmtail-month): **1.556% in November against 0.027% in October — a factor of 58 — and only 50
exceedances in total across January–July** (out of ≈1.9 × 10⁹ values in those months). November
corresponds to the dry-to-wet transition in this region **[SME: confirm regional seasonality]**.

*The concentration is sharper than a smooth seasonal mechanism predicts.* This is important for
interpretation. Because the selected day-of-year windows are wide (*h* = 45 modal, i.e. ±45 days),
any smoothly varying seasonal effect should be **smeared across October–December** rather than
confined to a single month. The observed near-binary October→November→December contrast is therefore
difficult to attribute to gradual regime blending alone, and points to something specific to the
November day-of-year recipes or fitted coefficients in the affected zones. The discriminating
diagnostic — not yet run — is to inspect the selected features, chosen *h*, and training residuals
for day-of-year ≈ 305–334 in the Amazon zones concerned, and to compare them with adjacent
day-of-year bands. **[TODO]**

*Not autoregressive drift.* Annual incidence is **non-monotonic** (0.2015%, 0.1696%, 0.0293%,
0.1299% for 2017–2020), and exceedances occur in short episodes — 40.6% are isolated single days,
mean run length 3.42 days, longest 36 days. Progressive error accumulation of the kind reported for
free-running autoregressive models [@gallusser2025] would produce growth with lead time and
lengthening runs; neither appears. This is consistent with the exogenous-forcing and
climatological-anchoring argument in @sec-discussion.

*Candidate mechanism.* A regime-dependent breakdown of the Tmin–Td coupling remains the leading
physical explanation, with the caveat above that it does not by itself account for the sharpness. @althoff2022
demonstrate that the Tmin-to-Td correction reverses sign between wet and dry seasons in a tropical
seasonal biome, and @forster2016 note that Tmin decouples from ambient moisture under cloudiness and
advection. Our selected windows are wide (*h* = 45 modal, @sec-results-selection), so a
transition-month day-of-year is fitted jointly with adjacent, moisture-abundant days; the resulting
slope, applied at the transition, over-predicts Td. This failure mode is not novel to this study:
@chabotcouture2014 report the same class of artefact in dew-point interpolation — interpolated Td
exceeding interpolated air temperature, implying RH > 100% — and recommend capping. Independent
evidence that late-season Amazon humidity is changing in ways a stationary mapping would miss comes
from rising dry-season vapour pressure deficit [@mu2025] and observed vertical drying over
deforested Amazonia [@hierro2025].

*A cap at Td ≤ Tmin is not viable.* We tested it: 79.6% of all predicted values exceed the same-day
Tmin, by a mean of 3.0 °C — and so does the *observed* gridded Td, since the Td = Tmin baseline has
a bias of −2.13 °C over this domain. Capping at Tmin would therefore alter 79.6% of the product with
a mean shift of 2.38 °C, which is not a correction but a distortion. The warm-tail values are
nonetheless extreme on this measure too: all of them exceed same-day Tmin, by a mean of 11.4 °C
against the 3.0 °C typical excess. A bound on the *excess* (Td ≤ Tmin + k) or on daily maximum
temperature is therefore worth evaluating, as is refitting the affected zones with explicit wet/dry
stratification. **[TODO]**

*Open question.* November 2019 incidence is roughly seven times lower than November 2017, pointing
to modulation by interannual climate variability (ENSO is the obvious candidate); this is untested.
**[TODO]**

No correction is applied in the product as it stands (@fig-warmtail, @fig-warmtail-month).

![Warm-tail exceedances by month of year. Left: pooled 2017–2020. Right: by year, showing that the
November spike recurs annually while its magnitude varies by a factor of
seven.](figures/F5_warm_tail_month_of_year.png){#fig-warmtail-month}

![Warm tail: value distribution, spatial location of affected cells, and monthly
incidence.](figures/F4_warm_tail_panel.png){#fig-warmtail}

**Regional pattern at the seam.** Panel B of @fig-seam shows a coherent regional signal (warmer
southern Andes, cooler northern Amazon). Because no observed Td exists after 2016, that figure alone
cannot separate a genuine 2017–2020 climate anomaly from regional model bias. The bound comes from
@sec-results-validation, where regional errors were measured directly on held-out years. **[SME]**

**Shared covariates.** Gridded Td and Tmin share LST and elevation predictors in their construction,
so validation against gridded Td may flatter the mapping relative to an independent reference.

**No station-level validation.** The target is the gridded product being extended, which is the
correct reference for this task, but it means the result inherits any bias of that product.
Station-level evaluation is out of scope here and is the natural next step. **[TODO]**

**Autoregressive horizon.** Skill decays with lead time; 2020 predictions rest on a longer recursive
chain than 2017. The lead-time curve quantifies this to four years, the length of the actual gap.

**Faint circular features** visible in @fig-seam appear in the observed-only control panel as well
and are therefore attributable to station influence in the underlying PISCO regression-kriging, not
to this method.

## Data and code availability {#sec-availability}

- **Code.** `HPC_code_tunning/` — selection (`selection.py`), training (`train_zoned.py`),
  autoregressive forecast (`forecast_zoned.py`), production fill (`fill_zoned.py`), validation
  (`backtest.py`, `select_backtest.py`, `effect_sizes.py`).
- **Product.** 2017–2020 gap-filled Td, 8,192 bucket files.
- **Figure and diagnostic scripts.** `reports/paper/scripts/` — QC, the three figure builders, and
  the warm-tail diagnostics, each reproducing specific numbers and figures in this manuscript.
- **Literature provenance.** `.asta/` holds the retrieved search and extraction records backing the
  citations added in @sec-discussion, so each may be traced to its source record.

## AI-use disclosure {#sec-ai-disclosure}

In accordance with CIP's Acceptable Use and Privacy policy: the analysis pipeline, validation
harness, production fill driver and figures described here were developed and executed with
AI assistance (Anthropic Claude, via Claude Code), under the direction and review of the author.
The AI assistant wrote and ran analysis code, produced the figures, and drafted this manuscript.
No confidential, personal, or unpublished third-party data was provided to the assistant; all
inputs are institutional gridded climate products.

**All quantitative results reported here are pending SME validation** (@sec-signoff). Numbers were
read directly from the recorded outputs of the runs cited, not reproduced from memory.
